Night-time or waking up in the dark

I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay
constantly check body for signs of danger or injury

issues.item: Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
issues.explanation: The trigger pattern is not very coherent for a captivity presentation as written: time-of-day could fit, but 'feeling happy or relaxed' and especially 'talks or photos about snakes' imply very different trigger themes without any supporting memory or appraisal content linking them to the captivity trauma.

issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: Threat items mainly describe interpersonal pursuit/external danger (hypervigilance, checking if someone is following me, unsafe at night). That could fit captivity, but it is not well matched to the selected snake-related trigger or to body-monitoring for injury, producing a fragmented threat picture.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: 'I am not sure my life is worth living anymore' is much more severe and somewhat qualitatively different from the other negative appraisal items, which focus on helplessness and being unable to cope with trauma thoughts. It may occur in PTSD, but here it is weakly integrated with the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: 'Constantly check body for signs of danger or injury' fits health/injury threat, but the threat items emphasize pursuit and ambush, while the triggers emphasize time-of-day, relaxation, and snakes. This coping strategy is therefore poorly linked to the rest of the formulation and symptom pattern.

vignette: Vikram Mehta, sixty-four, had been walking home from his wife Priya’s family gathering when three men forced him into the back of a van. They drove through the evening until the engine cut in an abandoned industrial lot, dragging him into a windowless storage room and bolting the heavy metal door. For six hours, Vikram sat on the cold concrete floor in absolute darkness. His captors spoke in low voices near the entrance, but the most piercing detail was how one of them periodically struck a length of pipe against the wall, replicating the rhythmic slither of a snake, while repeatedly warning him that venomous creatures lived in the walls and would strike if he tried to escape. When the lock finally turned and dawn light spilled through the crack, Vikram stumbled out, his shoulders rigid, convinced the confinement was only temporarily over. In the months that followed, the memory of that room did not settle into a narrative. Instead, it returned in abrupt, unmanageable fragments. Whenever the clock reached 10:45 in the evening, the exact hour the van had parked, Vikram’s breathing would shorten and his palms would grow damp. He turned away from any conversation or photograph involving reptiles, his gaze fixing on the floor the moment a snake appeared on a television or a phone screen. Sleep became an ordeal he could not complete. He would lie in his bedroom long after Priya had fallen asleep, pulling the blankets over his shoulders but keeping his eyes open, certain that darkness itself had become a threshold he must not cross. When he finally allowed himself to close his eyes, he would jolt awake within minutes, immediately running his fingers over his arms, legs, and neck to check for bruises or bites, scanning his own skin for signs of injury. Alongside this, he found himself unable to feel secure after the sun went down, a heavier vigilance replacing the relative calm of daylight. His employment at a regional distribution warehouse soon mirrored the conditions he had fled. The facility operated overnight, and Vikram navigated the high aisles with a rigid posture, his shoulders locked, constantly glancing over his shoulder to ensure no one was trailing him. At the loading bay, he would pause between conveyor belts and quietly ask the night supervisor, “Just tell me, am I safe here? Are there any cameras or exits I missed?” The reassurance brought a temporary dip in his pulse, but the feeling never fully settled. He moved through the warehouse floor with a heightened alertness, his eyes tracking every door opening, every shadow cast by stacked pallets. He could no longer tolerate the quiet stretches between shifts, his mind fixed on the certainty that bad things could arrive without warning and he would be powerless to stop them. To keep the memory at bay, he had learned not to think about it at all, changing the subject when others mentioned his missing weeks and keeping his radio on loud during long drives, certain that any quiet moment would let the room return. The weight of those parallel experiences slowly drained the color from his days. He began to wonder if the man who had walked home that evening was still anywhere inside him, his hands shaking during dinner, his thoughts fixed on the fear that his life had lost its direction. What finally brought him to this clinic was a moment in the warehouse freezer aisle, where the temperature dropped and the overhead lights flickered. He had stood frozen for twenty minutes, paralyzed by the certainty that he was running out of time. He knew he could no longer outrun the hours or the dark. He had come to this office hoping to find a way to stop scanning his own skin for wounds that were already gone, and to understand why the man who shared his bed sometimes felt like a stranger.
